activities.title: What happens when the dependency changes?

content.title: What happens when the dependency changes?
content.text:
Suppose `roomId` changes from `general` to `travel`.

A simplified sequence is:

**cleanup old synchronization → setup new synchronization**

The old room should stop being active before the new room becomes the current synchronization target.

options.text: The Effect reads `roomId` but claims it never depends on `roomId`.
Empty arrays automatically track every value.

feedback.correct: The dependency list needs to describe the reactive values that the Effect reads. Otherwise the synchronization can become stale.
feedback.incorrect: The dependency list needs to describe the reactive values that the Effect reads. Otherwise the synchronization can become stale.

content.title: Cleanup must mirror setup
content.text:
If an Effect starts something that stays active, ask what should stop it.

Start:

```jsx
const id = setInterval(doWork, 1000);
```

Cleanup:

```jsx
clearInterval(id);
```

Start:

```jsx
window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize);
```

Cleanup:

```jsx
window.removeEventListener("resize", handleResize);
```

The pairing is not ceremony. It defines the boundary of the synchronization.

options.text: A cleanup function that removes the listener.
A new state variable for every resize event.

feedback.correct: The Effect starts a long-lived browser subscription. It should return cleanup that removes that same subscription.
feedback.incorrect: The Effect starts a long-lived browser subscription. It should return cleanup that removes that same subscription.

content.title: The smallest correct dependency list
Common trap: the infinite loop
Development behavior
content.text:
In development, React may run an Effect's setup and cleanup more than once while checking whether the synchronization is correctly mirrored.

That is useful evidence.

If repeated setup/cleanup breaks the component, the synchronization probably is not being started and stopped cleanly.

content.question:
An Effect does all three of these:

- starts a browser subscription,
- reads `roomId`,
- needs to stop the subscription when `roomId` changes or the component leaves.

Which shape is most appropriate?

feedback.correct: The synchronization uses `roomId`, so it belongs in dependencies, and cleanup must stop the work that the Effect started.
feedback.incorrect: The synchronization uses `roomId`, so it belongs in dependencies, and cleanup must stop the work that the Effect started.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** An Effect is a synchronization process with a start, a set of reactive inputs, and—when needed—a stop.
**Senior habit:** Read an Effect as a contract: “Given these reactive values, keep this external system synchronized, and clean it up when the relationship changes.”
nextSteps: Repair a stale dependency, add cleanup to a browser subscription, and explain why an Effect that updates the same state it watches may be a sign of a wrong design.
